I just recently learned (from @David Renshaw's post) about https://eq677.icarm.cloud/, which I thought was pretty cool. It got me wondering, given that this final boss has lasted so long, if it might be worth making a dedicated "graph" to explore which relations are connected to each other, all under the assumption of finiteness + obeying 677?

A few times people talked about studying "pairwise" implications (like, do equations A and B together imply C, even with A and B individually do not), and while I think it was thrown around as an idea and the numbers weren't totally unreasonable, no one got super excited about it either because it was going to be much bigger and, maybe, more tedious.

In principle, if we start with finite+677 as assumptions, a lot of the graph already collapses (every equation that finite+677 implies is now 'trivial'!) and the graph should be quite a bit smaller!

My belief is that, if we explore this restricted space somewhat, then we can get a clearer picture of what equations do or don't point us towards 255. I think that a _lot_ of the knowledge has already been built, in somewhat scattered comments on the zulip. And https://eq677.icarm.cloud/ obviously has most of the counterexamples we would need to quickly refute constructions.
If people would be enthusiastic about this, I could start trying to spin up the appropriate stuff in a branch of the repo.

Follow up thought: we could choose to "truncate" the graph by 255, that is, if eqX and eqY both imply eq255, then we stop caring about comparing eqX and eqY to each other. This would also shrink it.

In that case, given the large number of easy collapses to expect, it might be worth aiming immediately for all order 5 laws. Not sure.

@Alex Meiburg For your information, one of my undergraduate research students has been exploring the implication graph for conjunctions of rules, and has made some good progress so far. We are not planning to focus on the 677->255 problem, so your proposed project would probably not overlap with what she has done so far.

Oh, that's great to hear someone is working on it! :) I was worried that idea that that idea had died (or rather, slumbered indefinitely).

The curious kid in me is eager to hear all about it and what's been working well or not and the progress! But, I also recognize that maybe I'd better not ask, and it's all too easy for such projects to get sniped.

But if you have any lessons for working with "one equation modulo another assumption" that you think would be useful for this targeted problem, I'd love to hear.
Alex I would definitely contribute to any public project that was moving toward solving this implication.
You should make a directed hypergraph, not a digraph, right

Directed hypergraph if it was looking at conjunctions of rules, right? And so looking at a bunch of equations 'assuming finite+677' would be really statements about conjunctions of rules, yeah. But my point is that if this is a constant extra assumption that we're tracking, then we can just as well treat it as a digraph, which is maybe easier to wrangle the data around. In particular, the existing code for tracking transitive closures and so on will all still work.
Well, here's a first step: bumping the Lean/Mathlib versions for the first time in just about a year. Big bump it was. :)

@Alex Meiburg Well, this was already under the assumption of finite+677. If you have R1 + R2 +...+Rk => R' where the rules R1....Rk are minimal (known) to imply R', then you'd have a directed hyperedge. One might also wish to have the target be expansive, so that you have a single hyperedge from {R1,...,Rk} to {R'1,....,R'n} to capture all the implications, rather than one for each implication for that set of assumptions (i.e. the source set).

The natural set-up (which may or may not be practical) is to consider conjunctions of arbitrary numbers of equations, their equivalence classes, and their whole implication graph. I've done this recently for a collection of 47 inequivalent quasigroup equations, and it's not as exponential as it looks: instead of getting the naive number 2472^{47}247 of conjunctions (all subsets), they collapse to just 114.

With Jose Brox we're halfway done with classifying all equivalence classes of conjunctions of equations of order up to 4 in associative magmas (aka semigroups), so it's the exact analogue of this thread for E4512 instead of E677. There are 122 equivalence classes of semigroup equations of order ≤4, and 456 equivalence classes of arbitrary conjunctions thereof (including the 122).

There were some discussions on conjunctions at #Equational > Search space for (EqX ∧ EqY) → EqZ some time back. There, we determined all conjunctions of equations of order at most 2, and I continued a bit at the time, finding that there are <5000 equivalence classes of conjunctions of magma equations of order at most 3 (I had a more precise value, which I cannot find again now). At order 4 the situation seemed hopeless: one way to put a lower bound on the number of classes is to consider a small number of test magmas MiM_iMi​, then for each equation EEE consider the set SE={i∣Mi⊨E}S_E = \{i\mid M_i\models E\}SE​={i∣Mi​⊨E}, and compute all intersections of these sets. Even with such a basic tool I was finding at least millions of classes, with no end in sight.

@Pace Nielsen it might be useful to coordinate: I certainly don't want to «scoop» your student.

The basic functionality seems like a go!

https://github.com/Timeroot/equational_theories/commit/a09763f6b36b60ae8b9e9a9ca5c3918a1186d882

I have one conjunction implication proof (677+8+finite -> 255), and the magmas up to size 11 in there (with pointers to the ICARM website ... although the lists of which magmas they do/don't satisfy isn't complete, I just put in a few by hand). When I added the implication the number of unresolved went down, and when I added the Facts the refuted number went up. :)

Corresponding to the 438 magmas in the database, I have now generated 438 files analogous to equational_theories/Generated/All4x4Tables/Refutation1.lean listing the complete set of equations they obey or disobey, out of the 1415 representatives of equivalence classes (instead of the full redundant set of 4694 equations). I'm thinking this should help with keeping Lean verification short enough. Are you ok with assuming this reduction from 4694 eqs to their equivalence classes?
Definitely, I'm taking that as input when I'm computing what's missing. We don't need to list all 4694!
And, nice -- that was fast! :)

See https://github.com/Timeroot/equational_theories/pull/3 for a draft pull request consisting only of the list of files, not properly integrated in the main Lean files (hence not properly tested). I likely have no time in the next week so feel free to pick up the commit or the files and do something else with them.

These were all assuming finiteness, yeah? Do you have a sense how many used finiteness?
Very nice results

Btw, for me, I'd be perfectly happy with just saying that "once we know EqX ∧ E677 -> Eq255, and EqY ∧ E677 -> Eq255, then we don't care about whether EqX ∧ E677 -> EqY or EqY ∧ E677 -> EqX". In that sense, everything implying 255 would become one 'equivalence class'.

The reasoning being, we're trying to map out the 'boundary' of equations which would imply 255, so that we know what properties we must avoid (if we want to construct a counterexample), or so that we build up more and more equations implied by Eq677 (that might eventually lead us to Eq255).

Of course I think it's nice to record any extra facts as we encounter them, but in terms of the number to target, I think it's fine to skip those implications... what do you think? Or, maybe you already did the same thing in your calculation -- I notice that 255 lists no known implications, but also no unknown implications... :)
(deleted)

The unknown implication you're expecting to see and don't see is between 1 (meaning E1∧E677, which is just E677) and 255 (meaning E255∧E677), which is absent because for incorrect reasons I have made my code skip the three known consequences of E677 (1, 614, 677).

There are two interesting approaches: focus on the E677-E255 "boundary" as you say and try to go to higher-order equations as well, or consider the whole conjunction implication semi-lattice. The second approach should lead to many open questions of difficulties that would range from "just use bijectivity of left multiplications" to "discover new methods to prove finite implications" or "find new ways to build finite countermodels" in the context of E677 magmas.

Regarding arbitrary conjunctions, the appropriate data structure for "all possible relationships" can definitely get a bit hairy. I've been playing with that for another project (categorizing different axioms of infinity over Zermelo set theory by implication strength), and I've abandoned trying to think about it as a graph in the general case. Instead, I just have a SAT solver enumerate all assignments, then add new clauses to whittle it down each time I find a new constraint. Ultimately, it should enumerate precisely the assignments that have a model.
(The end result would be a minimized CNF with all the constraints + proofs, alongside a big list of satisfiable assignments with models + proofs.)

I have thought a bit about E2⇔E75, E75 says that left-multiplication is 3-periodic. I convinced myself that there are no models coming from the near-field constructions that satisfy both. I know that there had been a systematic search of translation-invariant models with involutive left-multiplication, can this be easily adapted to translation-invariant models with left-multiplication 3-periodic?

I managed to adapt Rudi's dpll to search to translation-invariant models with 3-periodic left-multiplication, if I didn't mess up, there are no models (of Eq677 + Eq75) of size <= 42. I think we have a full classification of translation invariant models (just of Eq677) of size <= 37, so this is not too much of an improvement.

Note that E677+E75+finiteness (as left-quasigroup) implies idempotence E3 x◇x=x by your favorite ATP. Next, consider any x, y such that y◇x=x. By known E677 consequences, one gets y=(x◇x)◇x, equal to x by idempotence. Contrapositively, for x≠y one has y◇x≠x. Thus, the orbits of LyL_yLy​ are all of size 3 except Ly(y)=yL_y(y)=yLy​(y)=y. A finite E75+E677 magma must have size 3k+13k+13k+1 and each left multiplication has the same structure of a fixed point and k 3-cycles. Maybe this helps the search.
This model of size 321 satisfies E677 + E513 (left multiplication is 4-periodic), but not E384 := x ◇ y = (y ◇ x) ◇ x.

I believe this was an unknown implication in the graph constructed so far. The construction is closely related to the one of #Equational > ✔ FINITE: 677 -> 255 @ 💬, now with an affine extension of size 64 = 4*16 over the base 5 \ idempotents, using a S(2,5,65) model to glue in the extension over the idempotents with an extra point.

This model of size 249 satisfies E264 (right mutliplication is three-periodic), but not Equation4293[x ◇ (x ◇ y) = y ◇ (y ◇ x)]. It is a F8\mathbf{F}_8F8​ linear extension over (5*x - 4*y)%31 \ idempotents, gluing in the model of size 9 with an extra point over the idempotents.

I am pretty sure that there is a model of size 31^3 = 29791 that satisfies E264 and is idempotent (so we also get E1232), but still does not satisfy Equation4293. I am not sure whether it makes sense to submit this as a multiplication table to the database.
A rough calculation says that such text file will have size around 40GB. Maybe the maintainer should either make a more compact format, or reject the whole file :thinking:

I merged it, and added the size 249 model. Unfortunately it was so big that decideFin! was really really stuggling, I waited 10 minutes to no avail. I replaced it with native_decide as a workaround. This was forbidden with equational_result: so, I modified that. Declaring @[equational_result native] means that it should allow native_decide usage. This is, I hope, an acceptable compromise where we want to avoid native_decide where possible, but at the same time some of the very large magmas constructed seem to require it.

In principle we could eventually of course add more 'explicit' constructions of these magmas from their smaller subparts, which would allow more efficient symbolic proofs.
